chapters.title: Chapter 5: Scaling Playbook: Growing AUM Without Killing the Edge

lessons.title: Diversifying Across Strategies to Reduce Single-Strategy Capacity Dependence

children.text: Chapter 4 estimated capacity for one strategy at a time. This chapter is about scaling past what any single strategy can hold, and the first, most powerful tool for that is refreshingly simple: run more than one strategy.
The Basic Idea: Sum Capacities, Not Average Them

If Strategy A has a theoretical capacity of Rs 15 crore and Strategy B, using a genuinely different signal and universe, has a capacity of Rs 20 crore, running both together can support roughly Rs 35 crore, not somewhere between the two. This only holds if the two strategies are not meaningfully competing for the same liquidity or crowding the same trades, which turns out to be a real condition worth checking, not something you can assume from the strategies simply looking different on paper.
The Catch: Not All "Different" Strategies Are Actually Different

markDefs.definition: How much two strategies' actual traded positions coincide in the same names at the same time, distinct from how correlated their returns are. Two strategies can have low return correlation while still sharing heavy position overlap.

children.text: Low return correlation is necessary but not sufficient. What actually matters for capacity is

, whether the two strategies end up holding the same names at the same time. Two strategies built on entirely different logic can still both gravitate toward the same handful of small-cap names that look attractive to more than one screen at once, quietly sharing the exact liquidity pool and crowding risk that diversification was supposed to avoid.

body.caption: Return correlation alone is not enough

cells: Genuine diversification, capacities can reasonably be summed
Deceptive, returns look independent but liquidity and crowding risk are still shared
Unusual, worth investigating why returns move together despite different positions
Not really a second strategy, more a variant of the first

children.text: Take Strategy A, the Nifty 50 mean-reversion strategy from Chapter 4, theoretical capacity roughly Rs 17.4 crore. Pair it with Strategy B, a quality-and-value tilt on the Nifty Midcap 150, rebalanced quarterly, turnover roughly 4 times a year, holding around 20 positions. Using a typical midcap ADV of Rs 30 crore, daily volatility of 2%, and the same Y and cost budget used throughout this course, per-stock capacity works out to roughly Rs 3.33 crore, and total capacity across 20 positions to roughly Rs 66.7 crore.

body.text: This pairing works because the two strategies differ on the dimensions that actually matter for capacity, not just in name. Different universe, large-cap versus midcap. Different turnover, 25 times a year versus 4. Different signal, short-term reversion versus a slower quality-and-value tilt. Overlap between the two books is plausibly low, which is precisely the condition the earlier table flagged as necessary before capacities can be added together with any confidence.

body.title: Combine Two Independent Capacities
body.prompt: Two genuinely independent strategies, low return correlation and low position overlap, have theoretical capacities of Rs 25 crore and Rs 40 crore. What is their combined theoretical capacity, in Rs Cr?
body.explanation: Genuinely independent capacities add: Rs 25 Cr + Rs 40 Cr = Rs 65 Cr. The common mistake is to assume some kind of averaging or diminishing combination, but independence is precisely what allows simple addition here.

children.text: Indian Context: The Rise of Multi-Sleeve AIFs

A growing number of Indian quant AIFs and PMS structures now run exactly this kind of sleeve approach: a large, low-turnover, high-capacity anchor sleeve holding the bulk of AUM, alongside one or more smaller, higher-turnover satellite sleeves that contribute a disproportionate share of alpha relative to their size. It is a direct, practical response to everything Chapter 4 established, since no single high-turnover strategy could responsibly hold the fund's full AUM on its own.

body.text: Diversifying across strategies does not average out capacity constraints, it adds capacities together, but only when the strategies are different where it actually counts: universe, turnover, and position overlap, not just in the story told about them.

points: Running multiple genuinely independent strategies can sum their individual capacities, allowing total AUM far beyond what any one strategy could responsibly hold alone.

Low return correlation is not sufficient evidence of genuine diversification for capacity purposes, position overlap must also be checked, since two strategies can move independently in returns while sharing the same crowded liquidity.
A useful capacity-diversification test looks at both return correlation and position overlap together, treating high overlap as a warning regardless of how uncorrelated the returns appear.
Multi-sleeve structures, pairing a low-turnover, high-capacity anchor with smaller high-turnover satellites, are a direct, practical response to the capacity limits Chapter 4 established.
